title: In 1859, the Sun Set Telegraph Wires on Fire and Lit Up Cuba at Night

scenes.text: In 1859, the Sun set telegraph wires on fire from 93 million miles away.
A huge eruption hurled charged particles at Earth. They arrived in under a day.
Telegraph machines sparked. Operators got shocked. In some offices the paper caught fire.
In Boston, operators unplugged their batteries and kept sending. The sky was powering the wires.
Northern lights blazed over Cuba. People in Boston read newspapers by the glow.
Today, the bill would be up to two trillion dollars. And the Sun does this about once every 500 years.

description:
On September 1 and 2, 1859, the Carrington Event, the strongest solar storm on record, sent electric currents through telegraph wires: machines sparked, operators were shocked, and paper caught fire in some offices.
Auroras were seen as far south as Cuba and Jamaica, people read newspapers by their light, and Boston operators sent messages with the batteries unplugged. A 2008 US National Academy of Sciences report estimated a repeat today could cost one to two trillion dollars.
Would you want to see the aurora over the tropics, knowing what it meant?
thumbnail_text: THE SUN SET WIRES ON FIRE
first_comment: Ice cores suggest a storm this strong hits Earth roughly once every 500 years. What would you do for a week with no power, GPS or internet?
